extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, formal-methods users, and developers/users of proof assistants (people learning or using Metamath)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and technical description for writing, encoding, and verifying formal proofs in the Metamath language and for maintaining / using Metamath databases (e.g., set.mm). Covers language syntax, proof format, substitution checking, database/explorer usage, and tooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: archiving and verifying mathematical proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath is a formal language and an associated computer program (a proof assistant) for archiving and verifying mathematical proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Databases of proved theorems cover many fields (logic, set theory, number theory, algebra, topology, analysis). Use Metamath to store machine-checkable proofs and browse using the Metamath website Explorer interfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic-agnostic metalanguage
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath language is a metalanguage for formal systems and has no specific logic embedded in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metamath's design allows encoding different logical systems (first-order, higher-order, Hilbert systems, etc.) because inference rules are merely asserted as axioms or proved later; choose the axioms/inference rules appropriate to the formal system you want to represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design emphasis on simplicity and single substitution-based checking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath language design is focused on simplicity. Proofs are checked using an algorithm based on variable substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity means Metamath uses a minimal set of built-in mechanisms; more complex constructs (e.g., proper substitution) are derived instead of built-in. This leads to very small verifiers and many independent implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional distinct-variable provisos
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution algorithm has optional provisos for what variables must remain distinct after a substitution is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encoding axioms or rules that require variable distinctness, include distinct variable conditions so the checker enforces them during substitution/unification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax: comments, statement terminator, and symbol declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments are enclosed in $( ... $). The end of a statement is denoted by $.. The set of symbols usable in formulas is declared using $c (constant symbols) and $v (variable symbols) statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these token conventions exactly in .mm files. Example from page: $( Declare the constant symbols we will use $) $c 0 + = -> ( ) term wff |- $. and $( Declare the metavariables we will use $) $v t r s P Q $.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula grammar via $f (floating) and $a (assertion) statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The grammar for formulas is specified using a combination of $f (floating (variable-type) hypotheses) and $a (axiomatic assertion) statements. Each statement is given a name so it can be referred to in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use $f to declare types for metavariables (e.g., tt $f term t $) and $a to declare syntactic patterns or axiom schemas (e.g., tze $a term 0 $). Names (labels) are used as proof references.

rubrics_metrics.name: $e essential hypotheses and block scoping with ${ and $}
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms and rules of inference are specified with $a statements along with ${ and $} for block scoping and optional $e (essential hypotheses) statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ${ $} blocks to group hypotheses and $e to mark premises that are essential for derived assertions (example given for defining modus ponens). Proper grouping ensures the intended inference structure and scoping of local hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single $a construct for syntactic rules, axiom schemas, and inference rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A single construct, $a statements, is used to capture syntactic rules, axiom schemas, and rules of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides flexibility similar to higher-order frameworks while avoiding a complex type system. Encode both axioms and inference patterns using $a (possibly with $e and ${ $}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem and proof representation: $p and $=
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems (and derived rules) are stated with $p statements; their proofs are introduced with $=. A $p statement includes both the theorem and its proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs in .mm files are sequences of referenced labels and/or raw expressions; the $= section contains the proof steps; you may also provide an 'essential' form that elides syntactic bookkeeping for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential form of proofs for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'essential' form of the proof elides syntactic details, leaving a more conventional presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the detailed machine-checkable proof in the $= section, and optionally include a condensed essential proof (sequence of used labels) that is easier for humans to read and understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single substitution rule for all proof steps
rubrics_metrics.description: All Metamath proof steps use a single substitution rule, which is just the simple replacement of a variable with an expression and not the proper substitution described in predicate-calculus literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat substitution as the primitive inference mechanism; more sophisticated notions (proper substitution, capture-avoidance) are implemented at the database level as derived constructs or via distinct-variable provisos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification and type/class checking during substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: When checking a substitution, Metamath attempts to unify the assertion pattern with the target expression and must check that syntactic/type rules are respected (e.g., that unified expression has the required type class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof steps are validated by unification of metavariables to expressions and ensuring the resulting substitutions respect the declared types/classes and distinct-variable constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof verification workflow supported by the Metamath program
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program can read a Metamath database into memory, verify the proofs of a database, modify the database (in particular by adding proofs), and write them back to storage. It has a prove command that enables users to enter a proof, along with mechanisms to search for existing proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Metamath CLI for verification and proof entry; the program can also export statements in human formats (HTML, TeX). Search facilities help locate reusable theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Output and tooling interoperability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program can convert statements to HTML or TeX notation; many other programs can process Metamath databases (at least 19 known proof verifiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the ecosystem: multiple independent verifiers and frontends (mmverify.py, Ghilbert, Bourbaki, Hmm, Mmj2, Mmide, etc.) exist because of Metamath's simple core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Databases (.mm) and Explorer interfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Metamath databases (.mm files) have an associated interface called an 'Explorer', which allows interactive navigation of statements and proofs on the website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish databases with an Explorer when possible for better usability. Explorers (like the Metamath Proof Explorer) provide friendly browsing of statements, proofs, and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common use of Hilbert systems and canonical databases (set.mm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most databases use a Hilbert system of formal deduction though this is not a requirement. The Metamath Proof Explorer (set.mm) is based on classical first-order logic and ZFC set theory (with Tarski–Grothendieck when needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing mathematics, set.mm is the canonical, long-maintained database; choose the axiomatic base suitable for your development (classical, constructive, New Foundations, higher-order, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for different logical foundations via separate databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath can be used with different species of logic (Hilbert-style logics, sequent-based logics, lambda calculus). Separate databases implement different foundations (Intuitionistic Logic Explorer, New Foundations Explorer, Higher-Order Logic Explorer, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create or use specialized databases if your work requires a nonstandard foundation; explorers and database separation help manage differing axiomatic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: No built-in natural deduction—use conventions or nat.mm
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath provides no direct support for natural deduction systems; nat.mm formalizes natural deduction, and the set.mm database uses conventions enabling natural-deduction-like approaches within a Hilbert-style framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you prefer natural deduction, use nat.mm or follow established set.mm conventions to emulate natural deduction patterns while remaining compatible with Metamath checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tooling / editors: Mmj2 and alternate proof-entry modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors like Mmj2 provide a graphical user interface allowing forward or backward proof entry and a real grammar parser; Metamath itself typically allows entering proofs backward by theorem names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use GUI tools (Mmj2, Mmide, Milpgame, etc.) for more comfortable proof entry and visualization; be aware of differences—Mmj2 supports forward entry and parsing, which Metamath's original tools do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal verifier implementations are feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementations such as mmverify.py (≈500 lines of Python) demonstrate that very small proof checkers can implement the Metamath design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The minimal core and substitution-based checking make it practical to implement lightweight verifiers for experimentation, teaching, or integration into other systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking to literature and pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath Proof Explorer references many textbooks and is intended for people studying mathematics who want to verify that proved assertions match the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing or studying theorems, consult the referenced textbooks linked in explorers to ensure definitions and theorems align with standard treatments; use the Explorer as a pedagogical aid.
